content:
1	Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in
     2	 Financial Services
     3	 The financial industry’s adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) is
     4	 evolving as financial firms employ ever greater levels of technology and automation to deliver
     5	 services. Expanding on earlier models of quantitative analysis, AI/ML has often been adopted in
     6	 finance to solve discrete challenges, such as maximizing profit and minimizing risk. Yet the
     7	 industry’s adoption of the newer technology also occurs against perceptions that are steeped in
     8	 tradition and historical financial regulation, and regulators want to ensure that the technology
     9	 does not sidestep regulations frequently described as technology neutral.
    10	 Technological advances in computer hardware, capacity, and data storage—which permit the collection
    11	and analysis of
    12	 data—helped fuel the development and use of AI/ML technologies in finance. Unlike older algorithms
    13	that automated
    14	 human-coded rules, new AI models can “learn” by themselves and make inferences and recommendations
    15	not identified by
    16	 modelers in advance. This shift in technology has also enabled the use of new types of data
    17	including alternative data (i.e.,
    18	 data that the consumer credit bureaus do not traditionally use), unstructured data (images or
    19	social media posts, etc.), and
    20	 unlabeled information data—which, when combined, extend the technologies’ uses to new financial
    21	services or products.
    22	 Different parts of the financial services industry have adopted AI/ML technology to varying degrees
    23	and for various
    24	 purposes. Some uses of AI/ML include powering chatbots in customer service functions, identifying
    25	investment opportunities
    26	 and/or executing trades, augmenting lending models or (more sparingly) making lending decisions,
    27	and identifying and
    28	 preventing fraud. The extent to which a sector or firm adopts various technologies reflects a
    29	variety of factors, including a
    30	 firm’s ability to fund internal development and regulatory requirements.
    31	 The increased use of AI/ML to deliver financial services has attracted attention and led to
    32	numerous policy issues and
    33	 subsequent policy actions. Such policy actions culminated in (1) the establishment of a task force
    34	on AI in the 116
    35	 th Congress
    36	 and the more recent working group in the House Committee on Financial Services in the 118th and (2)
    37	2019 and 2023
    38	 executive orders. The evolving legislative and regulatory framework regarding AI/ML use in finance
    39	is likely, at least in part,
    40	 to influence the development of AI/ML financial services applications. Various financial regulators
    41	have indicated that
    42	 regulated entities are subject to the full range of laws and regulations regardless of the
    43	technology used. Additionally, some
    44	 regulators have identified regulations and issued guidance of particular relevance to financial
    45	firms employing AI/ML
    46	 technologies.
    47	 Financial industry policymakers face competing pressures. Financial service providers and
    48	technology companies are likely
    49	 to continue adopting and promoting AI/ML to save time and money and promote accessibility,
    50	accuracy, and regulatory
    51	 compliance. However, challenges and risks in the form of bias, potential for systemic risk and
    52	manipulation, affordability,
    53	 and consequences for employment remain. Determining whether the existing regulatory structure is
    54	sufficient—or whether
    55	 one that is more closely tailored to the technological capacities of the evolving technology is
    56	necessary—has emerged as a
    57	 key consideration. Should Congress consider the legislative framework governing AI/ML in finance,
    58	industry and consumers
    59	 alike will expect that it weighs the benefits of innovation with existing and potential future
    60	challenges and risks.

Unlike older algorithms that automated human-coded rules, new AI models can "learn" by themselves and make inferences and recommendations not identified by modelers in advance. This capability, combined with new data types—alternative data, unstructured data, and unlabeled information—has extended AI/ML's uses "to new financial services or products."

The article lists specific purposes: "powering chatbots in customer service functions, identifying investment opportunities and/or executing trades, augmenting lending models or (more sparingly) making lending decisions, and identifying and preventing fraud."

Additionally, the article states that financial service providers are likely to continue adopting AI/ML "to save time and money and promote accessibility, accuracy, and regulatory compliance."
